# Data, Annotation, and Ground Truth {#sec-data-annotation}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** Every number on this page was measured on the same
Turkish product-review corpus and the same 40,000/10,000 split used in
@sec-bake-off, with `scikit-learn` 1.9.0, NumPy 2.5.2 and pandas 3.0.5 on
Python 3.12.13. Two results are hand audits — readings of 140 Turkish reviews
by one person, with the criteria written down before the reading began. Treat
those two as one careful reader's judgement rather than as a measurement.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- read a sample of your own data and classify what you find into label errors, schema failures, and model errors — and act differently on each;
- write an annotation guideline that two strangers can apply to the same text and reach the same answer;
- compute inter-annotator agreement, and recognise when a 93% agreement score is telling you almost nothing;
- predict which direction of label noise will hurt you, and by how much, before you spend the annotation budget;
- build splits that do not leak, and measure what a leak is worth to your reported score.

## The number you have been trusting

@sec-bake-off ended with a leaderboard. Tf-idf over word 1–2 grams, fed to a balanced logistic regression, scored **92.57% accuracy and 76.21 macro-F1**. Bag of words scored 73.51. Averaged word2vec scored 61.39. The chapter's conclusion was that representation matters, that the ordering was stable, and that you should reach for the sparse baseline first.

::: {#gloss-gold-standard .column-margin .term-gloss}
**gold standard** — the labels everyone agrees to treat as correct when
scoring a model. Treating them as correct is a decision, not a fact, and
this chapter is about what that decision costs. [↩](#term-gold-standard){.term-back}
:::

Every one of those numbers was computed by comparing the model's output against a column called `sentiment` — the [gold standard](#gloss-gold-standard){#term-gold-standard .term-ref} for the whole leaderboard. Not once did we ask where that column came from, who wrote it, what question they were answering, or whether they were right.

This chapter asks. The setup is deliberately narrow: the representation is frozen at the @sec-bake-off winner, the split is the same, the seed is the same. The only thing that varies is the labels. That isolation is the whole point — when the score moves, you know exactly why.

What comes out is uncomfortable. A 2% error rate in the *test* labels drags the leaderboard's top entry below the score its bag-of-words rival earned on *clean* labels — not because the model changed, but because the ruler did. Note the shape of that comparison, because it is the honest one: two conditions with differently labelled test sets, not a rank reversal on a shared one. Scoring both models on the same noisy labels would answer a different question, and this chapter does not answer it. Half of the model's most confident "mistakes" turn out not to be mistakes at all: they are texts that a single binary label cannot describe. And 1,000 clean labels tie with 40,000 labels at 10% noise; at 20% noise, 500 clean labels beat all 40,000.

::: {.column-margin}
The corpus is the same one as in @sec-bake-off: 235,165 Turkish product reviews, 93.7% of them labelled positive. The imbalance is not incidental to this chapter — it is the reason most of the results look the way they do.
:::

**What we will look at.** Where a label comes from and what each step in its
manufacture can break. Then the two hours that repay themselves fastest —
reading a hundred rows yourself, and computing agreement properly. Then the
things that inflate a score without improving a model: a schema that cannot
describe the text, noise in the labels, and leaks between the splits. We
finish with what to do when you cannot hand-label at all, and where the effort
is actually best spent.

## Where a label actually comes from

A label is manufactured. Someone decided what the categories are, someone wrote instructions, someone read a text and pressed a key, and something aggregated the results. Each step is a place where the label can stop meaning what you think it means.

Everything downstream of the stored label — your training run, your leaderboard, your production monitoring — sees only the last box. The five failure modes underneath it are invisible by the time the data reaches you. The numbers are the ones measured later in this chapter on the review corpus.
:::

::::

The last box is the trap. By the time a dataset is a parquet file with a `label` column, the disagreement, the hard cases, and the annotator who was on their fourth hour have all been compressed into a single integer. Nothing in the file tells you which integers were easy.

### The questions to ask before you use a dataset

Before any modelling, answer these six. Write down the ones you cannot answer — the gaps are the finding.

1. **Who produced the text?** Not "the internet". Which platform, which population, which time window. The review corpus is people who chose to write a review after a purchase, which is not the same population as people who bought.
2. **Who produced the labels?** Platform metadata, crowdworkers, domain experts, or a model? Star ratings converted to sentiment are metadata, not annotation, and they carry the rating scale's own biases. Crowdsourced labels are not automatically worse than expert ones — @snow2008cheap showed that averaging a handful of non-expert judgements matches expert quality on several tasks — but "cheap and good" depends on the task being one where a non-expert can answer at all.
3. **What question were they answering?** "Is this review positive?" and "Would you buy this product?" and "Is this customer satisfied?" produce different labels on the same text.
4. **What licence, and does it cover your use?** Research-only is a real restriction. So is a licence that permits redistribution of the text but not of derived models.
5. **What consent existed?** Public availability is not consent. A user writing a product review did not agree to be training data, whatever the terms of service say.
6. **What is missing?** Which reviews were deleted, filtered, or never written. This is the hardest one and the one most worth attempting. @dodge2021documenting did it for C4, one of the most-used web corpora in the field, and found that the blocklist used to "clean" it had disproportionately removed text about and by minority groups. Nobody intended that; nobody had looked.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Licensing: what an engineer needs to know

Before any of that, a question that can stop a project after it ships rather
than before it starts: are you allowed to use this data at all?

**Public is not free.** "I could download it" and "I am permitted to train on it" are different claims. Scraped-from-the-web corpora frequently carry no licence at all, which means the default applies: the text is copyrighted by whoever wrote it.

**The licence travels.** If a dataset is CC BY-NC-SA, a model trained on it may inherit obligations depending on jurisdiction and on how much of the data the model memorises. This is genuinely unsettled law, which is itself the reason to be conservative in anything you ship.

**Provenance is a deliverable.** Record, at minimum: source URL, download date, licence text, and the exact filtering you applied. @longpre2024audit audited 1,800+ popular text datasets and found licence information missing or wrong for a large fraction of them — including datasets used in production. If you did not record it at download time, you will not be able to reconstruct it.

**Copyright is not the only regime.** If the text can be linked to a person — and a product review often can — you are simultaneously in a personal-data regime, and that one carries an erasure right: KVKK Articles 7 and 11 in Turkey, GDPR Article 17 in the EU. Consent is not the only legal basis, and "the user made it public" is one of the others — KVKK Article 5(2)(d) allows processing data the person has made public themselves — but that basis is read narrowly, as covering uses in line with the purpose for which the person published it, so a review posted to inform other shoppers does not automatically become model-training material. "I already trained on it" is not an answer to a deletion request, which is the practical reason to keep the row-id-to-source mapping you would otherwise be tempted to discard. And if what you build is high-risk under the EU AI Act, its Article 10 turns most of this chapter into a compliance obligation rather than good practice: documented provenance, examination for bias, and a stated governance process for the training, validation and test sets. @sec-governance-kvkk works through the obligations and the dates.
:::

## Read a hundred rows. Yourself. {#sec-random-audit}

The single most valuable hour in a data project costs nothing and requires no code beyond a random sample. Draw 100 rows from your test set, read them with the label visible, and classify what you see.

I drew 100 rows from the 10,000-row test split with seed 42 and read all of them. The criteria were fixed before reading:

- **error** — the gold label contradicts the text;
- **undecidable** — a single binary label is not determined by the text;
- **ok** — everything else.

I split `ok` in two during the reading, which is a deviation from the
pre-registered scheme and is recorded here for exactly that reason:
**arguable** for rows where the gold label is defensible but I would have chosen
the other one, and plain `ok` for the rest. The `arguable` count is therefore a
post-hoc category and carries less weight than the other three.

The result:

```text
### random 100 test rows, read by hand

errors (gold contradicts the text)          0
undecidable (binary label not determined)   7
   ... of which "not yet received"          3
arguable (defensible either way)            9
positive labels in the sample              98
```

Zero outright errors in 100 draws. With zero hits, the rule of three gives an approximate one-sided 95% upper confidence bound of 3/n: the data are **consistent with an error rate up to about 3%**, and rule nothing below that out. It is not a measurement that the rate is under 3%, and 100 draws cannot distinguish 0.1% from 2%. Under a uniform prior the posterior
mean for zero hits in 100 draws is $1/(n+2) \approx 1\%$, which is the number
to carry forward. That is a good corpus by the standards of public sentiment data.

The seven undecidable rows are the interesting ones, because they are not errors. Test row 4745 reads, in full:

> `sipariş verdim umarım tez ulaşır :)` — "I placed the order, hope it arrives fast :)"

Gold label: positive. The reviewer has not received the product. There is no product verdict in this text at all; there is a smiley and an expression of hope. Two of the other six are the same shape ("I just ordered it, judging by the reviews…", "it will probably arrive tomorrow"). One arrived used and scratched, but the reviewer says the product itself is good — a verdict on the *delivery* pointing the opposite way from the verdict on the *product*. Of the remaining three, one is a proverb about doors, one offers only a suggestion ("it would be better in liquid form"), and one is the string `seat leon st 1.6tdi` and nothing else.

A binary positive/negative schema has no cell for any of these. The annotator did not fail — the schema did. Hold onto that distinction; the rest of the chapter keeps returning to it.

::: {.column-margin}
Ninety-eight of the hundred were positive, against a corpus rate of 93.7%. That is within sampling noise for n = 100, but it is a reminder that a 100-row sample of a skewed corpus tells you almost nothing about the minority class. To audit the minority class, sample it separately.
:::

## The schema does more damage than the annotators

If the schema is where the damage is, it should be visible at scale — not just in a hundred rows one person happened to read.

So how would you look for it in 10,000? You need something that marks the reviews a binary label cannot describe, and you need it computable without reading anything. Turkish gives us one almost for free: the contrastive connectives *ama*, *fakat*, *ancak*, *lakin* — all roughly "but".

A caveat the rest of this section rests on: this is a screen, not a parser, and
its precision is unmeasured. *Ancak* also means "only" or "barely" — *ancak 3
günde geldi* is a statement about delivery time, not a contrast — and the rule
misses *gerçi*, *ne var ki* and *buna rağmen* entirely. So 20.03% is neither an
upper nor a lower bound — it has errors in both directions, and the true
contrastive share could sit either side of it. What it is: the share matching
this screening rule, whose precision and recall nobody has measured. Reading
fifty random matches would measure the precision — though not the recall — in ten minutes. The rule earns its place because the finding is the
*difference between the two groups*, which survives a fair amount of slop in
either. A review containing one of them is likely to be making two claims at once.

```python
import re
# tr_lower is the Turkish-aware lowercaser from @sec-bake-off (İ->i, I->ı)
CONTRAST = re.compile(r"\b(ama|fakat|ancak|lakin)\b")
has_but = np.array([bool(CONTRAST.search(tr_lower(t))) for t in test.text])
```

**2,003 of the 10,000 test reviews (20.03%) contain one.** They behave differently from the rest in every way that matters:

| | "but" reviews | the rest |
|:---|---:|---:|
| share of test set | 20.03% | 79.97% |
| gold negative rate | 11.48% | 5.03% |
| model accuracy | 84.07 | 94.70 |
| model macro-F1 | 72.11 | 77.72 |
| model F1 (negative) | 53.84 | 58.27 |

: The same model, the same test set, split on one function word {tbl-colwidths="[40,30,30]"}

A fifth of the corpus is twice as likely to be negative and ten accuracy points harder. Two explanations are available and this measurement does not separate them: the label schema is being asked to compress two verdicts into one bit, and the model may simply be worse at these sentences. @sec-bake-off's evidence bears on the first only indirectly — the *ranking* of representations was stable, which is weaker than showing that no representation helps. What would separate them is an aspect-level annotation of the same rows, scoring product and delivery independently; if the model recovers both aspects correctly and only the single bit is wrong, the schema is the problem. That experiment has not been run here, so read the schema reading as the more likely of two rather than the established one.

Which fix applies follows from which explanation holds, so the aspect-level annotation above is what decides it. If the disagreement comes from the target definition, the fix is a richer schema (aspect-level labels: product / delivery / price / packaging, each with its own polarity) or an explicit rule in the guideline telling every annotator which clause wins. If it comes from the model reading these sentences badly, a better representation is exactly what helps — and nothing here rules that out.

The general form of this problem has a name: **annotation artifacts**. When a guideline pushes annotators toward a habit, models learn the habit instead of the task.

How far does that go? Further than it sounds. @gururangan2018annotation found that a well-known inference benchmark could be partly solved by reading the hypothesis sentence alone and ignoring the premise entirely — the annotators who wrote those sentences had tells, and the model found them.

@geva2019annotator pushed further still, and showed that models can identify *which annotator* wrote an item, with scores dropping when the test set comes from annotators not seen in training.

The practical consequence is uncomfortable. If the same small group labels your train and test splits, your evaluation is partly measuring how well you have memorised that group.

### What a usable guideline looks like

::: {#gloss-annotation-guideline .column-margin .term-gloss}
**annotation guideline** — the written rules that let a second person
label your data the way the first person did. Without one, "the labels"
means "whatever that particular person thought that particular week". [↩](#term-annotation-guideline){.term-back}
:::

Most [annotation guidelines](#gloss-annotation-guideline){#term-annotation-guideline .term-ref} fail the same way: they define the categories and stop. Definitions are the easy part. The hard part is the list of decided cases, because that is the only part that makes two strangers agree.

```text
### annotation guideline v1 — product review sentiment

TASK
  Label each review positive (1) or negative (0) according to the
  reviewer's verdict ON THE PRODUCT.

DECIDED CASES  (these override the definition above)
  1. Delivery, packaging, seller, and returns are NOT the product.
     "Fast shipping, product is useless"          -> 0
     "Shipping was late, the product is great"    -> 1
  2. Price complaints are NOT negative unless the reviewer says the
     product is not worth it.
     "Expensive but excellent"                    -> 1
     "Not worth this money"                       -> 0
  3. Mixed verdicts on the product: the FINAL clause wins.
     "Cuts well but the handle broke"             -> 0
     "The handle is cheap but it cuts very well"  -> 1
  4. Not yet received / no verdict given          -> SKIP (do not label)
  5. Truncated text: if the visible text contains a verdict, label it;
     otherwise SKIP.
  6. Negation is not a signal by itself. "fena değil" (not bad) is
     positive. "kötü değil ama almam" (not bad but I would not buy)
     is 0 by rule 3.

WHEN TO SKIP
  Use SKIP freely. A skipped item costs one row. A guessed item costs
  one row AND corrupts the agreement estimate.
```

Two properties make this usable. First, every decided case has a worked example on both sides, so an annotator matching by pattern gets it right without understanding the principle. Second, `SKIP` exists. Forcing a binary choice on undecidable items is how you manufacture the disagreement you will later blame on the annotators.

::: {.column-margin}
Rule 3 — "the final clause wins" — is arbitrary. That is fine, with one condition. A guideline needs to be *decidable and consistent* before anything else — an annotator must always be able to tell which rule applies, and must apply it the same way every time — because an arbitrary rule applied consistently produces learnable data and a principled rule applied inconsistently does not. But consistency is necessary, not sufficient: a guideline that is perfectly decidable and measures the wrong thing produces labels with excellent agreement and no bearing on your task. Ask both questions, in that order.
:::

## Agreement, and why 93% of it can be worthless

Reading a hundred rows tells you what *you* think. The next question is
whether anybody else would agree — and the standard way of answering it is
more misleading than not answering at all.

::: {#gloss-inter-annotator-agreement-iaa .column-margin .term-gloss}
**inter-annotator agreement (IAA)** — how often two people labelling the
same items independently choose the same label. It is the closest thing
you have to a measurement of whether the task is even well defined. [↩](#term-inter-annotator-agreement-iaa){.term-back}
:::

You cannot know your labels are good by looking at one annotator's output. You need a second opinion on the same items, and a number for how often the two opinions match — the [inter-annotator agreement](#gloss-inter-annotator-agreement-iaa){#term-inter-annotator-agreement-iaa .term-ref}.

I do not have a second human, so I built a second annotator that is honest about being crude: a lexicon rule, 36 positive phrases and 37 negative phrases, applied to all 10,000 test rows.

One caveat before the numbers, because it changes what the coefficient means.
Annotator B is not a second opinion in the sense inter-annotator agreement
requires: it is a rule written by someone who had already seen the gold labels,
so $\kappa(\text{A}, \text{B})$ measures *how well a lexicon approximates gold*,
not *whether the task is well defined*. Everything below about prevalence and
$p_e$ transfers to a genuine two-human table unchanged — the arithmetic does not
care where the second column came from — but the number 0.2698 is not a
human–human agreement figure and should not be quoted as one.

```python
def annotator_b(text):
    t = tr_lower(text)
    neg = any(p in t for p in NEG)
    pos = any(p in t for p in POS)
    if neg and not pos:
        return 0
    return 1          # default to the majority class, as a tired human would
```

Call the gold column annotator A and the rule annotator B. Their confusion table:

```text
### A (gold, rows) vs B (lexicon rule, columns), n = 10,000

                B: negative   B: positive
A: negative           141           491
A: positive           167          9201
```

Raw agreement is $(141 + 9201)/10000 = \mathbf{93.42\%}$. Written on a slide, that number ends the conversation: the annotators agree on 93 out of 100 items, the labels must be fine.

::: {#gloss-cohen-s-kappa .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Cohen's kappa** — agreement after subtracting the agreement two people
would have reached by guessing. When one label dominates, guessing alone
scores very high, which is why raw agreement makes you look good. [↩](#term-cohen-s-kappa){.term-back}
:::

That 93.42% is not as reassuring as it looks. Both annotators call almost everything positive, so most of that agreement is what two labellers with these rates would reach without reading anything — which is a statement about how informative the *agreement figure* is, not a verdict on whether the gold labels are correct. Nothing about a low kappa against a lexicon establishes that. [Cohen's kappa](#gloss-cohen-s-kappa){#term-cohen-s-kappa .term-ref} [@cohen1960coefficient] corrects for exactly this:

$$\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}$$

where $p_o$ is the observed agreement and $p_e$ is the agreement expected if both annotators labelled independently at their own base rates. Here $p_e = 0.9099$, and:

$$\kappa = \frac{0.9342 - 0.9099}{1 - 0.9099} = \mathbf{0.2698}$$

Krippendorff's alpha [@krippendorff2018content], which handles more than two annotators and missing values, gives 0.2655 on the same table — close enough to confirm the reading rather than to add information.

A kappa of 0.27 is, on the conventional (and arbitrary) scales, "fair". The useful reading is a comparison rather than a decomposition: **93.42 points of observed agreement against 90.99 that two annotators with these marginals would reach while labelling independently, leaving 2.43 points above that baseline.** Resist turning that into "90.99 points *were* chance": $p_e$ is the agreement expected under an independence null, not a measurable portion of what actually happened. A low kappa on a corpus this skewed is consistent with careless labelling and with careful labelling alike; the coefficient does not tell you which one you have.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The arithmetic of $p_e$, spelled out

That correction is doing all the work, so it is worth seeing exactly what it
computes rather than taking the number on trust.

$p_e$ is the probability that two independent annotators land on the same label by chance, given how often each of them uses each label.

Annotator A calls 632/10000 = 6.32% of items negative. Annotator B calls 308/10000 = 3.08% negative. So:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_e &= P(\text{both say negative}) + P(\text{both say positive}) \\
    &= (0.0632)(0.0308) + (0.9368)(0.9692) \\
    &= 0.00195 + 0.90795 \\
    &= 0.90989
\end{aligned}
$$

Almost all of $p_e$ — 0.908 of 0.910 — comes from the second term. Do the arithmetic with the real marginals rather than a round number, because the round number misleads: A calls 93.68% positive and B 96.92%, and two labellers with those rates, choosing independently, land on the same answer $0.9368 \times 0.9692 + 0.0632 \times 0.0308 = 0.910$ of the time *whatever the texts say*. (Two labellers at 90% would reach $0.9^2 + 0.1^2 = 0.82$, not 0.90 — the expected agreement is not the marginal.) Kappa's denominator, $1 - p_e = 0.09$, is the room left for genuine agreement, and the numerator, 0.0243, is how much of that room the annotators actually filled.

This is why kappa collapses on skewed tasks and why reporting raw agreement on a skewed task is close to dishonest. It is also why kappa is unstable there: the denominator is only 0.09, so every change in $p_o$ is multiplied by about eleven on its way into kappa, and a handful of items moving between cells swings the result by a lot. Report both numbers, plus the confusion table, and let the reader see the skew.

Cohen's kappa is defined for exactly two annotators. When you have three or more — the normal case once a crowd platform is involved — use Fleiss' kappa [@fleiss1971measuring], which is the generalisation of *Scott's pi* rather than of Cohen's: it computes $p_e$ from a **single marginal pooled across all annotators**, not from each annotator's own rates, and it does not require the same annotators to have labelled every item (it does assume every item received the same number of judgements). Krippendorff's alpha [@krippendorff2018content] takes the idea further, writing agreement as $\alpha = 1 - D_o/D_e$ — observed disagreement over expected disagreement — with a distance function you choose, so one coefficient covers nominal, ordinal and interval labels and tolerates missing judgements. The interpretation, and the skew problem, are unchanged for all three.

That difference between "each annotator's own rates" and "one pooled rate" is not bookkeeping; it is the second of kappa's two known pathologies, and this corpus shows it. See below.
:::

### The same annotators, a different number

If prevalence is doing the work, changing the prevalence should change the answer without changing either annotator. It does. Subsampling to a balanced set — all 632 gold negatives plus 632 random gold positives, n = 1,264:

```text
### the identical annotators, on a class-balanced subsample

                    full test set (n=10,000)   balanced (n=1,264)
raw agreement                       93.42%              60.28%
p_e                                 90.99%              50.00%
Cohen's kappa                        0.2698              0.2057
Krippendorff's alpha                 0.2655              0.0722
```

Raw agreement falls by 33 points. Neither annotator changed. The only thing that changed is the mix of items handed to them — and raw agreement, which most people read as a property of the annotators, turns out to be mostly a property of the sample.

The two chance-corrected coefficients also part company on the right-hand column, and that gap is the second half of the story. On the full set they agree (0.2698 against 0.2655); on the balanced subsample kappa is nearly three times alpha (0.2057 against 0.0722), from the same data. The mechanism is the one named two sections above: Cohen's kappa computes $p_e$ from **each annotator's own marginals**, while alpha and Scott's pi use a **single pooled marginal**. On the balanced subsample A is 50% negative by construction and B is roughly 12% — a large divergence in how often the two of them reach for the minority label. Divergent marginals *lower* Cohen's chance baseline (here to 0.50, against 0.57 for the pooled marginal), so the same observed agreement counts as further above chance; alpha's pooled baseline is not lowered by the divergence, so it does not give that credit.

So kappa has two known pathologies rather than one. It *collapses* when the classes are skewed — the prevalence paradox, which is the whole of the previous section — and it *inflates* when the annotators' marginals differ, the bias paradox [@feinstein1990high; @cicchetti1990high]. This corpus exhibits both, in the two columns of one table. Report kappa and alpha side by side precisely so the gap between them stays visible.

::: {.column-margin}
One number in that table is exact rather than measured, and the reason is worth a line. On the balanced subsample $p_e = 0.5000$ exactly, because when one annotator is a perfect 50/50 split the expected agreement is $0.5b + 0.5(1-b) = 0.5$ *whatever* the other annotator's rate $b$ is. Half the coefficient's denominator stops depending on B entirely.
:::

The same 2×2 table will also produce whatever answer you want, if you choose the coefficient after seeing them:

```text
### the identical 10,000-row table, five coefficients
raw agreement  p_o                    0.9342
Gwet's AC1                            0.9277
PABAK  (2*p_o - 1)                    0.8684
Cohen's kappa                         0.2698
Krippendorff's alpha                  0.2655
```

Not one of these is wrong. They differ because they make different assumptions about what "chance" means when one class dominates: kappa and alpha assume annotators guess at their observed rates and charge you for the skew; PABAK and AC1 assume they do not, and refuse to [@gwet2008computing]. Which is right depends on which null you think is the fair comparison for your task, not on diagnosing from the table whether anybody guessed. The coefficients differ in what they assume chance agreement *would* look like; none of them can tell you what the annotators were doing. [The same two annotators can be reported anywhere between 0.27 and 0.93.]{.hl} The honest report is the confusion table plus at least one chance-corrected number, with the choice stated.

There is a second lesson hiding in B's scores. Annotator B achieves **93.42% accuracy** against gold. @sec-bake-off's majority-class baseline — label everything positive, read nothing — achieves **93.68%**. B's hand-built lexicon, 73 phrases of careful Turkish, performs *worse than a constant*. On macro-F1 the picture is different (63.27 for B against 48.37 for the constant), which is the whole reason @sec-bake-off refused to report accuracy alone.

There is a third number worth reporting, and it is already on the page under a different name. **Specific agreement** — agreement restricted to one label, $2 n_{kk} / (n_{k\cdot} + n_{\cdot k})$ — is 96.55% on positive and **30.00%** on negative. That second figure is numerically identical to B's negative-class F1, because a binary F1 between two labellings *is* specific agreement. It localises the problem in one line that no single chance-corrected scalar can: these two annotators agree almost perfectly about praise and barely at all about complaint.

::: {.anlp-widget}

```{=html}
<div class="widget-title">What agreement is worth at a given prevalence</div>
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof prevalence = Inputs.range([0.02, 0.5], {step: 0.01, value: 0.063, label: "minority class share"})
viewof rawAgreement = Inputs.range([0.5, 1.0], {step: 0.005, value: 0.934, label: "raw agreement"})
viewof bias = Inputs.range([0.0, 1.0], {step: 0.05, value: 0.5, label: "B's minority rate ÷ A's"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
kappaOf = function (prev, obs, ratio) {
  const a = prev;
  const b = Math.min(0.999, Math.max(0.001, prev * ratio));
  // Not every (a, b, p_o) triple comes from a real 2x2 table. With minority
  // rates a and b, observed agreement is confined to |1-a-b| <= p_o <= 1-|a-b|.
  const lo = Math.abs(1 - a - b);
  const hi = 1 - Math.abs(a - b);
  const feasible = obs >= lo - 1e-9 && obs <= hi + 1e-9;
  const pe = a * b + (1 - a) * (1 - b);
  return {pe: pe, lo: lo, hi: hi, feasible: feasible,
          kappa: (!feasible || pe >= 0.9999) ? null : (obs - pe) / (1 - pe)};
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
kappaTable = kappaOf(prevalence, rawAgreement, bias)
```

```{ojs}

</table>`
```

Hold raw agreement fixed and slide the prevalence. The same 93.4% agreement is worth kappa ≈ 0.27 on this corpus and would be worth far less on a more skewed one — and rather more on a balanced one, provided the two annotators' rates stay close enough to reach that agreement at all. That proviso is doing real work: not every setting of the three sliders describes a table that can exist, and the widget refuses to invent a kappa where none does. The curve is drawn only over the prevalences the chosen agreement rate can actually arise from, which is why it covers a short arc rather than the whole axis. The hollow circle marks the measured point.

The verbal labels under the number — *slight*, *fair*, *moderate*, *substantial*, *almost perfect* — are @landis1977measurement's benchmark scale, and they are worth naming precisely because everyone uses them and almost nobody says where they come from. The authors proposed the bands as "clearly arbitrary" divisions for discussion, not as measured thresholds. Report the number and the interval; treat the adjective as a label for a conversation, never as a passing grade.

:::

### Adjudication

::: {#gloss-adjudication .column-margin .term-gloss}
**adjudication** — a third pass over the items two annotators disagreed
on, to settle them. Disagreements are not noise to be averaged away; they
are the places where the guideline is unclear. [↩](#term-adjudication){.term-back}
:::

Agreement measurement is diagnostic; [adjudication](#gloss-adjudication){#term-adjudication .term-ref} is the repair. The loop that works:

1. **Both annotators label the same 200 items, stratified toward the minority class.** Not a sample of each — the same items. And not a plain random 200: at this corpus's 6.3% minority share a random 200 contains about thirteen minority items, and kappa's entire numerator lives in those cells. Oversample the minority until the pilot is roughly balanced; you are estimating a coefficient, not a prevalence.
2. **Compute kappa with a bootstrap confidence interval, and the confusion table.** The interval is not optional at this size. A kappa's standard error depends on the marginals as well as the sample size, so bootstrap it rather than reaching for a formula — resampling this corpus's table gives about 0.02 at 10,000 items and about 0.14 for a plain random 200, which puts the 95% interval around a point estimate of 0.27 at roughly $[-0.02, 0.54]$: anything from "no agreement beyond chance" to "moderate". Stratifying pays here too: on a pilot of 100 gold-negative plus 100 gold-positive items, the same two annotators give a standard error of about 0.04 — and a different point estimate, around 0.21, because kappa depends on the sample's class mix, as the balanced-subsample table above showed. What to do with that interval is a decision you make before you look at it. Decide what agreement your task actually needs and stop only when the interval clears it; an interval that contains 0.4 proves nothing on its own, in either direction. A point estimate of 0.35 whose upper bound is 0.6 is not evidence of anything.

    ```python
    from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score
    rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
    idx = (rng.integers(0, len(a), len(a)) for _ in range(2000))
    boot = [cohen_kappa_score(a[i], b[i]) for i in idx]
    lo, hi = np.percentile(boot, [2.5, 97.5])
    ```

3. **Read every disagreement together.** Not to decide who was right, but to find out *why* they differed. Most disagreements cluster into three or four recurring situations.
4. **Add each situation to the guideline as a decided case with examples on both sides.** This is the deliverable.
5. **Re-annotate a fresh 200 and re-measure.** If kappa did not move, the problem is the schema, not the guideline.

The mistake is treating step 3 as a vote. Adjudicating item by item gets you 200 resolved items. Adjudicating *categories of disagreement* gets you a guideline that resolves the next 20,000.

### What to do with three annotators instead of two

Adjudication does not scale past a pilot, and the failure diagram at the top of this chapter named *collapse* — disagreement thrown away when the judgements are aggregated into one label — as its own failure mode without saying what to do about it. With a crowd you have several judgements per item and a choice about how to collapse them.

**Majority vote** is the default, and it is wrong whenever annotators differ in reliability: it gives the careless third voter the same weight as the careful first. **Latent-variable aggregation** [@dawid1979maximum] estimates each annotator's confusion matrix and the true label jointly by EM (expectation–maximisation: guess the true labels, re-estimate each annotator's error rates from the guesses, re-guess, and repeat until nothing changes), with no ground truth required — the same idea, a hidden true label plus a per-source reliability, underlies the label model in Snorkel-style weak supervision. And a third option, which this chapter's own findings argue for: **do not collapse at all.** Keep the vote distribution and train against a soft target — an item two of three annotators called positive gets the target "positive with probability 0.67" instead of a hard 1, and the loss rewards the model for matching that probability. On a corpus where a large share of confident disagreements turn out to be schema failures rather than mistakes, an item three annotators split 2–1 is carrying information about the task that a hard label deletes [@uma2021learning; @plank2022problem].

## Auditing labels at scale {#sec-audit}

You cannot read 40,000 rows. You can make the model tell you which ones to read.

The technique is out-of-fold prediction, the practical core of confident learning [@northcutt2021confident]. Fit on four folds, predict the fifth, repeat. Every training row now has a prediction from a model that never saw it. Where the model is confident in the *other* class, the label is a candidate for being wrong.

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold

skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
oof = np.zeros(len(y))
for a, b in skf.split(Xtr, y):
    oof[b] = clf().fit(Xtr[a], y[a]).predict_proba(Xtr[b])[:, 1]

# confidence that the stored label is wrong
wrong_conf = np.where(y == 1, 1 - oof, oof)
```

On the 40,000 training rows:

| threshold | rows flagged | share | gold positive | gold negative |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| > 0.50 | 3,026 | 7.57% | — | — |
| > 0.90 | 92 | 0.23% | 49 | 43 |
| > 0.95 | 34 | 0.09% | 20 | 14 |
| > 0.99 | 2 | 0.005% | — | — |

: Rows the model is confident are mislabelled {tbl-colwidths="[18,18,14,25,25]"}

Three things are worth noticing.

**The flags are class-balanced, the corpus is not.** At the 0.90 threshold, 43 of 92 flags are on gold-negative rows — 47% — in a corpus that is 6.3% negative. Per row, 1.70% of negative labels are flagged against 0.13% of positive ones — a negative label is *thirteen times* more likely to be flagged. That is where your annotation quality problem lives.

**Almost nothing is flagged at high confidence.** 92 rows out of 40,000. If you expected a 5% error rate you would expect 2,000. The technique finds errors the model can detect, which is a strict subset of errors that exist — it is blind to errors on texts it also finds hard.

**A flag is a request to read, not a verdict.** So I read them. I took the equivalent 40 highest-confidence flags on the *test* set — where a wrong label costs you a wrong leaderboard rather than a slightly worse model — and classified each by hand into: `error` (gold is wrong), `schema` (a single binary label cannot represent the text), or `model` (the label is defensible and the classifier is wrong).

```text
### 40 highest-confidence gold/model disagreements, test set, read by hand

error   (gold label is wrong)                        11    27.5%
schema  (binary label cannot represent the text)     20    50.0%
model   (label defensible, classifier wrong)          9    22.5%
                                                     --
data-side problems                                   31 / 40

schema breakdown:  mixed 12 · truncated 4 · lukewarm 3 · no verdict 1
```

**Thirty-one of forty are problems with the data, not the model** — but read that as a direction, not a rate. With $n = 40$ and a single unblinded reader (me, who had written the hypothesis), the 95% Wilson interval (a confidence interval for a proportion that stays sensible at small $n$) on the schema share runs from about 35% to 65%, and on the error share from 16% to 43%. Those two intervals overlap. The claim this measurement supports is "schema failure is a first-order category, comparable in size to outright error" — not "exactly half". A second reader on the same forty items, with kappa reported, would cost an hour and would settle it; I did not do that, and you should before you quote the number.

Four of the forty show what the categories mean:

- **Row 6874** (gold = negative, model p(positive) = 0.984). Clear praise, no reservations, labelled negative. A genuine error — someone pressed the wrong key.
- **Row 8356** (gold = positive, p = 0.059). *"yastıklar ince yeterli değil"* — "the pillows are thin, not enough." Labelled positive. Another genuine error.
- **Row 8006** (gold = positive, p = 0.034). The review praises the *returns process* at length and never says anything good about the product. The label is defensible under a "was this a good experience" reading; the model was fooled by the praise vocabulary. Model error — and exactly what decided case 1 in the guideline above exists to prevent.
- **Row 2544** (gold = positive). *"paketleme başarısız. ampüller fena değil"* — "packaging failed. the bulbs are not bad." Two verdicts, opposite directions, different aspects. Neither label is wrong. The schema is.

Five of the nine model errors turn on negation: *fena değil* ("not bad"), *özelliklerinin altında bir ürün değil* ("not a product below its specifications"), and one triple negation. A bag-of-n-grams model has no mechanism for scope of negation. Its word bigrams give it a two-word window — *fena değil* is itself a feature, useful only if that exact pair was frequent enough in training — but anything longer, like the second example, is just *değil* as a feature with a weight. That limitation is the subject of @sec-transformers.

### What cleaning actually bought

Given 92 suspect rows, the obvious next move is to remove them or flip them and retrain. Both were measured on the untouched test set:

```text
### repairs, judged on the test set that was never touched

                          acc    macro-F1   F1(neg)
baseline (no repair)     92.57      76.21     56.47
drop 92  (p > 0.90)      92.37      75.72     55.61
flip 92  (p > 0.90)      92.47      75.94     55.99
drop 34  (p > 0.95)      92.39      75.83     55.83
flip 34  (p > 0.95)      92.52      76.03     56.15
drop  2  (p > 0.99)      92.54      76.15     56.37
flip  2  (p > 0.99)      92.52      76.11     56.31
```

**No repair improved anything.** The largest movement is half a macro-F1 point, and it is worth being careful about how to read a table of small negatives: elsewhere in this chapter three seeds give a standard deviation up to 0.50 macro-F1, which is the size of the largest cell here. So do not read the individual drops as a downward *effect* — they are noise around zero, and the next paragraph says so. What the six conditions do rule out is a *large* gain: nothing here moved by more than half a point in either direction, so if confident learning helps on this corpus it helps by less than this design can see. Absence of a visible gain is not proof of no gain — the same uncertainty that stops you reading the drops as an effect stops you excluding a small improvement.

This is not a failure of the technique; it is the technique working correctly and telling you something you should want to hear. Two reasons:

1. **92 rows out of 40,000 is 0.23% of the training data.** Editing that few rows is unlikely to move a model trained on 40,000 examples — unlikely rather than impossible, since influence is not proportional to count and a handful of rows near the boundary can matter more than their share. The differences above are consistent with noise around zero.
2. **Half of what you would remove is not an error.** The hand audit says 50% of high-confidence flags are schema failures — texts with real, defensible labels that happen to be hard. Deleting them removes exactly the hard cases the model most needs to see. That fits the small pattern in the table — flipping (which keeps the row) edged out dropping (which removes it) at the 92- and 34-row thresholds — but the margins are 0.2–0.3 points and reverse at 2 rows, so treat it as consistent with the explanation rather than as evidence for it.

The value of the audit was never the retrained model. It was the finding that half the confusion is schema, which tells you to fix the guideline rather than the labels — a conclusion no automated cleaning pass would have reached. Automated flagging finds the rows; a human reading them produces the insight. @northcutt2021pervasive found label errors in the test sets of ten of the most-used ML benchmarks, and the important consequence there was also not "the models got better after cleaning" — it was that model rankings are fragile to test-label quality: scored against corrected labels, on ImageNet a ResNet-18 overtakes a ResNet-50 once the originally mislabelled examples make up just 6% more of the test set.

## What label noise costs, and in which direction

Suppose your annotation process has an error rate. How much does it cost? The honest answer is: it depends entirely on which direction the errors go, and the dependence is not subtle.

I corrupted the training labels at controlled rates under three regimes, retrained from scratch, and evaluated against the clean test set. Three seeds each; standard deviation never exceeded 0.50 macro-F1.

```text
### macro-F1, clean test set, model retrained at each rate
### rates are the share of the SOURCE class flipped; "symmetric" flips that share of EACH class

flip rate      0%     1%     2%     5%    10%    20%    30%    40%
symmetric   76.21  74.18  72.43  68.58  63.34  55.43  49.86  43.71
neg -> pos  76.21  76.14  76.29  76.27  76.42  76.85  77.12  76.47
pos -> neg  76.21  74.17  72.87  68.63  63.63  56.69  52.01  47.99
```

The middle row does not move. You can mislabel **forty percent of the negative class as positive** and lose nothing — at 30% it even reads slightly higher than baseline, which is noise, not a real gain. The bottom row loses 28 points over the same range.

```{=html}
  <text x="634" y="54"  class="t-xs t-b t-accent">neg → pos</text>
  <text x="634" y="68"  class="t-xs t-mono t-muted">76.47</text>
  <text x="634" y="196" class="t-xs t-b">pos → neg</text>
  <text x="634" y="210" class="t-xs t-mono t-muted">47.99</text>
  <text x="634" y="228" class="t-xs t-b t-rose">symmetric</text>
  <text x="634" y="242" class="t-xs t-mono t-muted">43.71</text>

  <rect x="70" y="284" width="640" height="52" rx="6" class="box-warm"/>
  <text x="82" y="301" class="t-xs t-b t-warm">why the flat line is flat</text>
  <text x="82" y="316" class="t-xs">flipping 40% of 2,529 negatives shrinks the minority class but leaves it pure;</text>
  <text x="82" y="330" class="t-xs">flipping 10% of 37,471 positives makes the negative class 59.7% garbage.</text>
</svg>
```

::: {.fig-cap}
Three noise regimes on the same 40,000 training rows, evaluated on the same clean test set, three seeds each. The direction of the error matters more than its rate — an asymmetry that follows entirely from the 93.7/6.3 [class imbalance](#gloss-class-imbalance){#term-class-imbalance .term-ref}.
:::

::::

::: {#gloss-class-imbalance .column-margin .term-gloss}
**class imbalance** — one label is far more common than the other. Here
93.7% of reviews are positive, so a model that answers "positive" every
time looks accurate while finding nothing. [↩](#term-class-imbalance){.term-back}
:::

The arithmetic behind the asymmetry is worth doing once, because it generalises to every imbalanced problem you will meet.

**neg → pos at 10%:** 253 of 2,529 negatives are relabelled positive. The positive class grows to 37,724, of which 253 are wrong — **0.67% contamination**. The negative class shrinks to 2,276 but every remaining member is correct. A smaller, pure minority class is still learnable.

**pos → neg at 10%:** 3,747 of 37,471 positives are relabelled negative. The negative class is now 2,529 correct plus 3,747 wrong — **59.7% garbage**. The model is fitting a class whose majority membership is noise. There is nothing to learn.

The same asymmetry appears at rates far too small to notice in a spreadsheet. At **1% pos → neg**, only 375 rows flip — one percent of the *positive class*, which is 0.94% of all training rows, a rate most teams would call excellent. But those 375 rows are **12.9% of everything now labelled negative** (375 of 2,904, the 2,529 real negatives plus the 375 arrivals), and they cost 2.04 macro-F1 points — more than the entire gap between bag of words and tf-idf unigrams in @sec-bake-off, which was 1.56.

Two rules follow, and they are the practically useful output of this section:

- **Measure your annotation error rate per class, and say which class the errors come *from*.** An overall 1% is meaningless, and the direction is the whole finding: errors that *turn minority rows into majority ones* barely registered here, while errors that *turn majority rows into minority ones* cost 12.58 points at the same 10% class-conditional rate. Name the source class and the target class every time, because "1% in the majority class" reads both ways and only one of them is the cheap one.
- **On a task this imbalanced, an unsure annotator applying the minority label is the expensive mistake.** That is the opposite of most people's instinct, which is to be generous with the interesting label. Two conditions on it, though: it follows from *this* imbalance and this cost structure, and it is not a licence to guess — the `SKIP` value and an adjudication pass are the better answer when the item is genuinely undecidable, which is what the guideline earlier in this chapter is for. Where a missed minority case is the expensive error — screening, safety, fraud — the arithmetic runs the other way and you should redo it.

::: {.column-margin}
This asymmetry is a property of the imbalance, not of sentiment. What carries over to any task where one class is 5–10% of the data — spam, fraud, medical screening, content moderation — is the *direction*: manufacturing minority labels costs more than erasing them. The size is a property of your classifier, your metric and your error mechanism, and has to be measured rather than read off this table. Theory for learning under class-conditional noise is surveyed in @frenay2014classification.

One caveat about how this noise was made, because it bounds every number above. These flips are **class-conditional**: chosen at a fixed rate, independent of the text. Real annotation error is not. A tired annotator does not get random items wrong; they get the *hard* ones wrong, so the errors concentrate exactly where the decision boundary already is. The audit earlier in this chapter shows it directly — the flagged rows are mixed, truncated and lukewarm reviews, not a random 0.23% of the corpus. Instance-dependent noise at the same nominal rate is measurably more damaging, because it moves the boundary rather than just blurring it [@wei2022learning]. The taxonomy is in @frenay2014classification, which separates noise independent of everything, noise depending on the class, and noise depending on the instance; this experiment is the middle one. So read these curves as the **mild case** rather than a bound: there is good reason to expect your real error rate to cost more than this, and no arithmetic here that says it cannot cost less.
:::

## Your test set is a ceiling, not a ruler

Everything so far corrupted *training* labels and measured on a clean test set. Now the reverse: one fixed model, trained once on clean data, evaluated against test labels of decreasing quality. The model never changes. Only the ruler does.

Note the change of denominator, because the word "noise" is doing different work in the two experiments. In the previous section a "1% flip rate" meant one percent *of the source class*. Here it means one percent *of all test rows*, flipped in whichever direction the row happened to be — at this corpus's balance, about 94 positives and 6 negatives per hundred flips. Uniform flipping is a controlled stress test, not a claim about how test labels actually go wrong — the margin note on instance-dependent noise at the end of the previous section applies here too, and real test errors concentrate on the hard rows.

```text
### one fixed model, corrupted test labels, mean of 5 seeds

test noise      acc   macro-F1   F1(neg)   sd(macro-F1)
### noise here = share of ALL test rows, flipped uniformly at random
    0%        92.57      76.21     56.47          0.00
    1%        91.73      74.68     53.90          0.23
    2%        90.85      73.13     51.31          0.12
    5%        88.31      69.41     45.36          0.17
   10%        84.19      64.79     38.66          0.24
   20%        75.48      57.00     28.82          0.36
```

Line these up against the @sec-bake-off leaderboard, which was computed on clean labels:

| system | macro-F1 |
|:---|---:|
| tf-idf 1–2 gram, clean test labels | 76.21 |
| tf-idf 1–2 gram, **1%** test-label noise | 74.68 |
| bag of words, clean test labels | 73.51 |
| tf-idf 1–2 gram, **2%** test-label noise | 73.13 |
| tf-idf unigram, clean test labels | 71.95 |
| tf-idf char\_wb 3–5, clean test labels | 70.39 |

: The @sec-bake-off leaderboard, interleaved with the same winner measured against noisier rulers {tbl-colwidths="[62,38]"}

**Two percent noise in the test labels is enough to erase the chapter-4 winner's reported margin over a rival measured on clean labels.** Not because it became worse — it is byte-for-byte the same model, making byte-for-byte the same predictions.

Read the table carefully, though, because it is easy to over-claim from it and the over-claim is instructive. Those rows are not all on the same ruler: 73.13 is the winner measured against noisy labels, 73.51 is bag-of-words measured against clean ones.

Resist the tempting repair, which is to say the ranking would have survived under a *common* noisy ruler. In expectation, for independent symmetric flips at rate $\eta < 0.5$, it does: a classifier's noisy accuracy is $\eta + (1 - 2\eta)\,a_{\text{clean}}$, which is increasing in $a_{\text{clean}}$, so the order is preserved on average. On one realised test set it need not be. Take 100 items where A is wrong only on item 3 and B only on items 1 and 2 — clean, A scores 99 and B 98. Flip the labels of items 1 and 2 and score both against *those* labels: A drops to 97 and B rises to 100. Same predictions, same corrupted ruler, reversed order. Whether it happens to your pair is an empirical question, and this experiment did not run it.

What this table actually shows is the danger of **cross-lab comparison**: your 73.13, measured on a test set with 2% label noise, is indistinguishable from someone else's 73.51 measured on a clean one, and neither paper reports its label quality. That is how a leaderboard inverts in the literature without a single model changing, and it is why "which test set, how clean" belongs in every comparison you make.

Three consequences:

**Your test labels decide what your score means.** With 2% test noise a classifier that is perfect *against the truth* scores 98% — and note that 98% is not a ceiling on the number: a model that has learned to reproduce the same errors your annotators made scores higher, while being worse. Once your model's error rate approaches your labels', the score stops tracking quality in either direction, and further improvement is invisible or, worse, penalised.

**Small differences on a noisy benchmark are not results.** If the test set has 1% label noise, a 1.5-point macro-F1 gap is inside the uncertainty the labels themselves contribute. @sec-bake-off's 15-point gaps survive this; a 0.4-point gap between two BERT variants on a public leaderboard frequently does not. @recht2019imagenet and @beyer2020imagenet document what happens when this is taken seriously on a famous benchmark.

**Spend disproportionately on the test set.** The training set can tolerate noise, especially in the majority class — the middle row of the previous section is the proof. The test set cannot tolerate any. If you have budget for 10,000 careful labels and 40,000 cheap ones, put the careful ones in test.

## Leakage: the errors that make you look good {#sec-leakage}

Everything so far has been about labels being *wrong*. This section is about a
failure with the opposite signature: the labels are right, the model is
honest, and the score is still a lie.

::: {#gloss-label-leakage .column-margin .term-gloss}
**label leakage** — when something in your input quietly carries the
answer, or when the same text sits in both training and test. The score
looks excellent right up to the day you deploy. [↩](#term-label-leakage){.term-back}
:::

Label noise makes your score worse than the truth. [Label leakage](#gloss-label-leakage){#term-label-leakage .term-ref} makes it better, which is why it survives so much longer.

The raw corpus has 235,165 rows, of which **1,657 are exact duplicate texts** (0.70%). @sec-bake-off de-duplicated before splitting. Suppose it had not:

```text
### split-before-dedup, the ordinary careless mistake

exact duplicate texts in the raw corpus        1,657   (0.70%)
test rows also present in train                   45   (0.45% of test)
near-duplicates after normalisation               34   (0.34% of test)

same model, same run:
  accuracy on the 45 leaked rows                93.33
  accuracy on the 9,955 clean rows              91.90
  macro-F1 on the leaked rows                   76.76
  macro-F1 on the clean rows                    74.08
```

A 2.68-point macro-F1 gap on rows the model had memorised. With n = 45 that gap is noisy, and 0.45% contamination is far too little to move the headline number. This corpus's leak is real but small. (The 74.08 here does not match the 76.21 baseline used elsewhere in the chapter because this run deliberately does *not* deduplicate before splitting — the number to compare it against is its own 76.76.)

Real corpora are frequently worse, and the effect scales in a way that is worth seeing directly. Copying a controlled fraction of the test set into training — precisely what a careless split does, just at a larger dose:

| test rows copied into train | accuracy | macro-F1 | F1 (negative) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0% | 92.57 | 76.21 | 56.47 |
| 1% | 92.57 | 76.27 | 56.60 |
| 2% | 92.62 | 76.41 | 56.86 |
| 5% | 92.65 | 76.53 | 57.08 |
| 10% | 92.82 | 77.14 | 58.20 |
| 25% | 93.33 | 78.59 | 60.82 |
| 50% | 94.00 | 80.89 | 65.07 |
| 100% | 95.62 | 85.89 | 74.17 |

: What leakage is worth, at controlled doses {tbl-colwidths="[34,22,22,22]"}

Read the curve as a diagnostic. **A 10% leak buys about one macro-F1 point** — well within the range of a genuine modelling improvement, and completely undetectable from the score alone. A 100% leak buys nearly ten points, which is the size of the gap between two chapters of legitimate work.

That is the danger. Leakage does not produce unbelievable numbers. It produces *believable* ones, slightly better than they should be, which is exactly the shape of a result you want to believe.

The near-duplicate check is more informative than the exact one. On the properly de-duplicated split of @sec-bake-off, normalising away case, punctuation and whitespace finds 34 test rows whose normalised form appears in training. Their macro-F1 is **67.62** against **76.23** on the rest — *lower*, not higher, because after de-duplication the surviving near-duplicates are mostly short generic fragments (*"güzel ürün"*, *"teşekkürler"*) that are genuinely ambiguous. Not every duplicate is a leak; some are just hard. The same caveat applies here: at n = 34 this gap is at least as noisy as the 45-row one — macro-F1 on thirty-four rows is close to meaningless. The direction is informative; the magnitude is not.

### The leaks worth checking for

In rough order of how often they bite:

1. **Exact duplicates across splits.** One line of pandas: `df.drop_duplicates(subset="text")` before splitting, never after.
2. **Near-duplicates.** Normalise case, punctuation and whitespace; then compare. For longer texts, compare the sets of overlapping word n-grams ("shingles") with Jaccard similarity — shared shingles divided by all shingles — or with MinHash, a fast approximation of it that scales to millions of documents.
3. **Group leakage.** Multiple reviews by the same user, multiple sentences from the same document, multiple images of the same patient. Split on the *group*, not the row. This is the leak that most often survives review, because the rows genuinely differ.
4. **Temporal leakage.** If your model will run on future data, your test set must be from the future. A random split lets the model see next month while predicting last month.
5. **Preprocessing leakage.** Fitting the vectoriser, the scaler, or the feature selector on all the data before splitting. In @sec-bake-off's pipeline, `vec.fit_transform(train)` then `vec.transform(test)` — never `fit` on the concatenation.
6. **Benchmark contamination.** Your public test set was on the web, and the pretrained model you are fine-tuning read the web. @kapoor2023leakage catalogue leakage across 17 scientific fields; @magar2022data and @oren2024proving develop tests for whether a specific benchmark is in a specific model's pretraining data. This becomes the central problem in @sec-llm-eval.

## Where to spend the next thousand labels

You have a budget. The two dials are how many labels you buy and how carefully each is produced. They trade off: careful labels cost more, so you get fewer. Which dial do you turn?

Before the grid, one paragraph on what "cost more" means, because there is a person on the other end of it. At a realistic 150–250 short reviews an hour, 40,000 labels is roughly 200 hours of somebody's attention. Three consequences follow, and they are engineering consequences and not only ethical ones. **Pay structure determines data quality**: piece-rate payment rewards speed, and speed produces exactly the fatigue slips this chapter's failure model names, so an hourly rate with a quality gate produces different data from the same instructions. **Task design is a working condition**: a guideline with `SKIP` and decided cases is both faster and less punishing than one that forces a binary choice on undecidable items — the same change that improves your kappa improves someone's day. And on some tasks — moderation, safety, abuse detection — **exposure is a real cost**, and a project that budgets annotator hours without budgeting rotation and support is under-costed rather than cheap [@gray2019ghost; @sambasivan2021everyone]. Record in your datasheet who labelled, how they were paid, and at what rate; @gebru2021datasheets asks for exactly this and almost nobody answers it.

The grid below trains the same model at seven budget sizes and six noise levels, three seeds each, and evaluates all 42 cells on the same clean test set.

```text
### macro-F1 by budget and label noise (clean test set, 3 seeds)

                 0%      5%     10%     20%     30%     40%
    500       59.44   58.56   55.57   51.18   47.40   42.12
  1,000       63.71   60.91   57.77   52.32   46.99   42.78
  2,500       68.76   64.17   60.03   53.36   48.23   42.93
  5,000       71.69   66.00   60.21   53.17   47.86   42.42
 10,000       73.72   66.47   61.81   54.46   48.53   42.88
 20,000       74.89   66.99   62.04   55.21   49.09   43.81
 40,000       76.21   68.18   63.20   55.74   49.34   44.16
```

Read across a row and you learn what noise costs. Read down a column and you learn what volume buys. Read diagonally and you get the finding:

- **1,000 clean labels scored slightly higher than 40,000 labels at 10% noise: 63.71 against 63.20.** Forty times the data, and it did not buy a higher mean — though at 0.51 points, with a seed-to-seed standard deviation of up to 0.50 elsewhere in this chapter, treat that pair as a tie rather than a win. The 20%-noise row below is the one that carries the argument.
- **500 clean labels (59.44) beat 40,000 labels at 20% noise (55.74).** Eighty times the data, and it loses by nearly four points.
- **Volume only pays when quality is high.** Going from 500 to 40,000 labels buys **16.77** macro-F1 points at 0% noise and **2.04** points at 40%. Scaling a broken annotation process is the most expensive way to accomplish nothing.
